title: End-User Engagement Is the Best Proof of Progress
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece argues that internal performance metrics — KPIs, OKRs, and similar operational indicators — can't fully capture organizational health on their own; the true test is how the end user experiences the enterprise. It catalogs a sprawling list of possible user-facing metrics (retention, churn, satisfaction, completion rates, and dozens more) to make the point that leaders willing to measure user experience have nearly limitless tools to do so. The article urges leaders to combine quantifiable user metrics with direct qualitative feedback — surveys, interviews, focus groups — to build a textured understanding of how users actually experience the organization, arguing that progress never happens exclusively inside an organization's own walls.
points: Internal metrics like KPIs and OKRs are treated as necessary but insufficient — user experience is named as the strongest proof of genuine organizational progress.
The article catalogs dozens of possible user-facing metrics, arguing the constraint on measuring user experience is imagination, not data availability.
Direct qualitative feedback (surveys, interviews, focus groups, support interactions) is recommended alongside quantitative metrics to build a "textured" understanding of the user.
The piece frames progress as something that "never occurs exclusively inside the walls of an organization," pushing leaders to look outward rather than only at internal dashboards.
quotes: If the user experience is not enhanced, elevated, or amplified by the improvements and changes directed at them, it really doesn’t matter what the internal metrics say.
Leaders and organizations who understand the power of the user experience go to great lengths to measure how users interface with the organization.
Because leaders can’t manage what they can’t measure, quantifiable indicators of the user experience and outcomes are also essential.
Because at the end of the day, it is users that determine how successful an enterprise is and will be.
Great leaders look outside, to users, to understand how effective the organization really is.
